title: Mud Carey, the band splitting and the new instruments
summary: Mud Carey replaces the drowned trumpeter, then the band breaks up; Valentine and his cousins form a new band and buy instruments, but members leave one by one.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Mud Carey came out, he used to come out, you know like on Saturdays night and play with him you see. But I tell you, now Mud Carey was a fellow, was more of a Dixieland player, you see. Yeah. Well them fellows were musical. They were strictly musical, them fellows there. All them fellows were realists, you know what I mean. Yeah. And so he'd come out on Saturdays and then he would always want the fellows to play in the style he played you see. You know what I mean. More live and jazzy like, you know what I mean. But the fellow wasn't so used to that because they strictly read music, you know what I'm talking about. So well finally they went on like that, the band went on and they played like that for a long time and so finally, you know again, the band split up. Well my cousin, well now we had a band ourselves you see, so my cousin, we organized a new band. So I got my cousin to play with me and so after I got my cousin to play with me, well the band had to split up you see. So what they did, Marshall organized a new band. He started teaching you see, youngsters you see, to teach me. Well that's a pretty good band for boys. Used to come all down here and play too you see. Used to come down, they had a great big band, all musicals you know what I mean. Well he used to come down here and go all over the country and play, Texas, different places you know. So well my cousin, he played drum with us, so he left and went to, he went to Baton Rouge, play with Toot Johnson. So well every now and then, every week, and like that, they used to send for him to come out and play. So finally after he started playing with them regular, he went up there and lived there. You see, he moved his family there and went to live there and he stayed there all the again until he died you see. So well our band, now when he left, you see we had bought, we had bought a whole lot of new instruments, a whole set of instruments. That Hall boy, Edmund Hall is the one, him and my cousin came down here and ordered the instruments at Groomhall. I had a Holton trumpet, we had a brand new Holton banjo, trombone, a whole lot of flit you know. So after this fella, after he came back, my cousin, they came back with all the instruments, brought all the instruments at night and all the boys out there you know. You know how some people be jealous you see. Man, when my cousin Edmund brought them instruments and pulled them out there, them fellas eyes stretched big like that you know. He said, how y'all gonna pay for them instruments? But we was getting paid to white. Oh we was getting paid to white, we had a good band. We were a good band, that's my mother say. We were a good band. We were a good band. So, alright. So we got the instruments. So finally we doing alright. We paid for the instruments and everything. So, alright. Edmund, he left, no the oldest brother left first, Robert left. He left the country and come down here. So after that Edmund, he left. So finally that left, Clowns playing the banjo with us you see. Well Clowns still stayed. So alright. So Clowns playing the banjo. He wasn't playing no saxophone, playing the banjo. So when you know again, he wanted to leave. So everybody leaving but me. See that left me. I was the last one. Did Herbert Hall play ever with you? No, no.
